opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to where value actually gets created. Over the past few years the industry poured enormous energy into the model layer: bigger models, better benchmarks, more compute. That work matters, and it gave us capabilities that were hard to imagine not long ago. But a model by itself is a bit like an engine sitting on the factory floor. It's impressive, but it doesn't take anyone anywhere until you build the car around it.

When you start from the application, you start from a real problem: a customer who needs to process documents faster, a developer who wants to ship code with fewer bugs, a company trying to make its support team more effective. That forces you to deal with the things that determine whether AI actually works in practice: latency, cost, reliability, data privacy, how the system fits into an existing workflow. Those constraints are often more important than a few points on a leaderboard.

There's also a feedback loop. Applications generate real usage, and real usage tells you what the models get wrong, what the infrastructure needs to handle, and where the bottlenecks really are. Without that signal you end up optimizing for things that look good in a paper but don't move the needle for users.

From my own experience on the infrastructure side, from frameworks to cloud platforms, the best infrastructure has always been shaped by demanding applications. The tools got better because people were trying to build real things with them and kept hitting walls. I think AI is now at that stage. The foundation is strong enough that the next wave of value will come from people who deeply understand a domain and use AI to rethink how the work gets done, not just bolt a chatbot onto an old process.

So for me, application-driven development isn't the opposite of fundamental research. It's what gives the research direction, and it's how AI goes from technically impressive to economically meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response says application usage reveals what models get wrong and where bottlenecks are, but does not state that iteration gradually reveals the technology’s actual capability boundaries.

r002.rationale: It advocates building real applications around AI, but does not state the sequence that after capability boundaries are understood, further progress requires integrating the technology into real products.

r003.rationale: It says the next wave of value will come from people who deeply understand a domain and use AI to rethink how work gets done, identifying application-side understanding as key to creating greater value.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that I've spent a lot of my career on the infrastructure side, building frameworks like Caffe and then working on the platforms at Facebook and Alibaba, and what I learned over and over is that infrastructure by itself doesn't create value. It only creates value when someone actually uses it to solve a problem they care about.

When we were building Caffe at Berkeley, the thing that made it take off wasn't that it was the most elegant framework. It was that people could pick it up and train an image classifier that afternoon and ship it. The applications pulled the technology forward. Every time someone hit a limitation, that became the next thing we fixed. So the feedback loop between real use and the underlying tech is where the progress came from.

I think the same dynamic is even more true with large models today. We have incredibly capable base models, and the capability gap between them is actually shrinking. What's not shrinking is the gap between "this model can do something impressive in a demo" and "this is embedded in a workflow where it saves a company real money or lets a person do something they couldn't do before." That last mile is where most of the value lives, and it's also where you learn what the models actually need to be good at.

If you start from the application, you discover very concrete things: latency matters more than you thought, the cost per token determines whether a feature is viable at all, the model needs to be reliable at the boring things rather than brilliant at the exciting things. Those constraints then shape what you build in the infrastructure layer. That's a big part of why we started Lepton AI focused on making it simple and cheap for people to actually deploy and run these models, rather than on training yet another foundation model.

So for me, application-driven development isn't about being less ambitious technically. It's the opposite. It's the only reliable way to figure out which technical problems are worth solving, and to make sure the enormous investment going into AI turns into something people actually feel in their daily lives.

r001.rationale: The response describes a feedback loop in which real use reveals limitations and drives fixes, communicating that iteration uncovers the technology’s capabilities and limits.

r002.rationale: It says embedding models in workflows creates value and helps reveal needs, but does not clearly state that once capability boundaries are understood, further progress requires integrating the technology into real products.

r003.rationale: The response says applications reveal concrete needs that shape infrastructure and calls application-driven development the reliable way to identify which technical problems are worth solving.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that a more capable model doesn’t automatically translate into a more useful product. You have to start with a concrete problem: What is someone trying to accomplish, and what would make that task easier or better?

Take an AI assistant for customer service. Answering a question fluently is only part of the job. It needs access to the right information, it needs to know when to hand things over to a person, and it needs to work within the company’s existing processes. Those requirements tell you what to improve in the model and what to build around it.

That’s why application-driven development matters. Real usage gives you a feedback loop. You discover which capabilities people actually need, where failures are costly, and whether an improvement is worth the additional latency or expense. Sometimes the biggest gain comes from a better model; sometimes it comes from better data or a simpler workflow.

Ultimately, the value of AI comes from helping people achieve something. Applications give us a way to measure that value and guide the technology toward it.

r001.rationale: The response says real usage reveals needed capabilities and failure points, but does not state that iteration gradually reveals an emerging technology’s capability boundaries.

r002.rationale: It describes building around models and using applications for feedback, but does not state that integrating the technology into real products is necessary for further progress once its boundaries are understood.

r003.rationale: It identifies starting from concrete user problems and understanding application needs as key to making AI useful, and says applications guide the technology toward greater value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think applications are where we discover what actually matters. You can improve a model’s benchmark score, but that doesn’t automatically mean you’ve made someone’s work easier or created a product they’ll pay for. To create value, you have to connect the technology to a real problem.

And that connection changes how you develop the technology. If you’re building an application, you start asking concrete questions: Is the answer reliable enough? Is the response fast enough? Can we deliver it at a cost that makes sense? Sometimes the bottleneck is model capability, but sometimes it’s the data, the infrastructure, or how the product fits into somebody’s workflow.

That’s why I see application development as a feedback loop. You put something in users’ hands, learn where it succeeds and fails, and use that information to guide the next technical improvement. Better technology enables new applications, and those applications tell us what technology we need next. That cycle is what turns AI capability into practical value.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning from user successes and failures, but does not clearly say that iteration gradually reveals the technology’s capability boundaries.

r002.rationale: It connects technology to real problems and products, but does not state that integrating it into products is required for further progress once its capability boundaries are understood.

r003.rationale: The response makes discovering real problems, workflow fit, and user feedback central to turning AI capability into practical value, communicating that understanding application needs is key.
